- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥0.7) and forecast shows a sharp upward spike, reduce the peak by 5–10% to avoid overreaction.  
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤-0.3) and forecast shows a sharp downward dip, avoid underreacting — slightly increase the trough by 3–5% to prevent premature bottoming.  
- If forecast consistently overshoots true values by >3% over 3–5 consecutive days, apply a “mean reversion” correction: subtract 1–2% from the next 3–5 forecasted days.  
- If sentiment is volatile (alternating ±0.3 or more) and forecast is erratic, smooth the forecast curve by averaging 3–5 adjacent points to reduce noise.  
- For horizon >15 days, if forecast is trending upward but sentiment is weak or neutral, reduce slope by 15–20% to reflect lack of momentum.  
- If forecast is consistently higher than true outcome in early days (1–5) and sentiment is positive, assume “sentiment-driven overconfidence” — reduce first 3–5 forecasted values by 2–4%.  
- If forecast is consistently lower than true outcome in late days (25–30) and sentiment is negative, assume “sentiment-driven pessimism” — increase last 3–5 forecasted values by 2–4%.
